question.title: Azure Database for MySQL
question.scenario: A company runs a popular WordPress site backed by MySQL. They want to migrate to Azure for better scalability and reduced management overhead while keeping MySQL as their database engine.
question.question-text: Which Azure service should they use for their MySQL database?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The company needs to keep MySQL as their engine. Which Azure service preserves engine compatibility rather than requiring a switch to a different database platform?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Database for MySQL (D) is a fully managed PaaS service running the MySQL community engine, providing automated backups, patching, HA, and scaling while maintaining full MySQL compatibility for WordPress. Azure SQL Database (A) uses the Microsoft SQL Server engine, which is incompatible with MySQL applications. Azure Cosmos DB (B) is a NoSQL database that does not support MySQL queries or the MySQL wire protocol. Azure Database for MariaDB (C) runs the MariaDB engine — while MariaDB forked from MySQL and shares some compatibility, WordPress specifically requires MySQL or its direct Flexible Server equivalent, and using MariaDB introduces unnecessary compatibility risk.

ul.li: Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server is the recommended deployment, offering same-zone and zone-redundant HA, stop/start capability for dev/test cost savings, and configurable maintenance windows.

WordPress is the most common use case for MySQL on Azure — the Azure Marketplace offers pre-configured WordPress on Azure App Service templates that automatically provision Azure Database for MySQL as the backend.

MySQL and MariaDB share a common heritage, but they have diverged: MariaDB includes unique storage engines (Aria, ColumnStore) while MySQL has features like the InnoDB Cluster. The DP-900 exam expects you to match MySQL applications to Azure Database for MySQL specifically.
Azure Database for MySQL supports read replicas for scaling read workloads, data-in replication from external MySQL servers for migration, and Private Link for secure VNet connectivity.

question.title: Cosmos DB API Selection
question.scenario: A team is building an application that stores product catalog data as JSON documents. They want to use familiar MongoDB query syntax and drivers because their developers have extensive MongoDB experience. They also want the benefits of Azure's managed services.
question.question-text: Which Azure Cosmos DB API should they choose?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The developers want to use their existing MongoDB query syntax and drivers. Think about which Cosmos DB API lets you keep your current wire protocol and tooling unchanged.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The API for MongoDB (D) provides wire protocol compatibility with MongoDB, allowing developers to use existing MongoDB drivers, tools (mongosh, Compass), and query syntax while benefiting from Cosmos DB's global distribution and SLAs. The API for NoSQL (A) is Cosmos DB's native API using SQL-like queries over JSON — it is powerful but would require the team to learn new query patterns instead of using their MongoDB expertise. The API for Table (B) is compatible with Azure Table Storage and uses key-value access patterns, not document queries. The API for Apache Cassandra (C) supports CQL (Cassandra Query Language) for wide-column workloads, not MongoDB document patterns.

ul.li: The Cosmos DB API for MongoDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 3.2, 3.6, 4.0, and 4.2, meaning existing applications can migrate by changing only the connection string — no code changes required for supported operations.

Choosing the right Cosmos DB API on the DP-900 exam: API for NoSQL (new apps, native Cosmos features), MongoDB (existing MongoDB apps), Cassandra (existing Cassandra apps), Gremlin (graph traversal), Table (migrating from Azure Table Storage).

All Cosmos DB APIs share the same underlying engine — choosing MongoDB API does not sacrifice performance, availability, or global distribution. The API choice determines the wire protocol and query language, not the storage or replication behavior.

For new applications with no existing database investment, Microsoft recommends the API for NoSQL because it provides the richest Cosmos DB feature set including full SQL query support, change feed, and integrated indexing policies.

question.title: Azure Cache for Redis
question.scenario: A web application experiences slow performance because it frequently queries the same data from the database. The team wants to store frequently accessed data in memory to reduce database load and improve response times.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides an in-memory data store for caching scenarios?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs an in-memory data store to cache frequently accessed data and reduce database round-trips. Which option is designed for caching rather than persistent primary storage?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Cache for Redis (B) is a fully managed in-memory data store based on open-source Redis, designed specifically for caching frequently accessed data to reduce database load and achieve sub-millisecond response times. Azure Cosmos DB (A) is a persistent NoSQL database — while it offers low latency, it is not an in-memory cache and is significantly more expensive for pure caching scenarios. Azure Table Storage (C) stores data on disk, not in memory, and does not provide the sub-millisecond access times needed for caching. Azure Blob Storage (D) is object storage for files and documents, completely unsuited for in-memory data caching.

ul.li: Azure Cache for Redis supports common caching patterns: cache-aside (application checks cache first, falls back to database on miss), write-through (writes go to both cache and database), and write-behind (writes go to cache immediately, asynchronously synced to database).

Beyond simple key-value caching, Redis supports rich data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and streams — enabling use cases like session state management, real-time leaderboards, rate limiting, and pub/sub messaging.

Azure Cache for Redis offers three tiers: Basic (single node, no SLA — development only), Standard (replicated primary/secondary with SLA), and Premium (clustering, persistence, VNet isolation, geo-replication for enterprise workloads).
On the DP-900 exam, Redis is the answer when the scenario mentions: in-memory, caching, session state, reducing database load, or sub-millisecond latency for repeated data access patterns.

question.title: Modern Data Warehouse Architecture
question.scenario: An enterprise is designing their analytics architecture. They plan to ingest raw data into a data lake, use data pipelines to transform and load data into a data warehouse, and then serve it to Power BI for visualization.
question.question-text: What is this integrated approach to analytics architecture commonly called?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The architecture combines a data lake, transformation pipelines, a warehouse, and BI visualization. What is this end-to-end analytics pattern called when it updates a traditional approach with cloud-native components?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A modern data warehouse (B) is Microsoft's reference architecture that integrates a data lake (raw storage), data pipelines (ETL/ELT transformation), a data warehouse (curated analytical storage), and a BI tool like Power BI (visualization) into a cohesive analytics solution — exactly what the scenario describes. A Lambda architecture (A) specifically separates processing into a batch layer and a speed layer for real-time, merging results at a serving layer — the scenario does not describe this dual-path pattern. A Kappa architecture (C) processes all data through a single streaming pipeline, eliminating the batch layer — not matching the described batch-oriented pipeline flow. A Medallion architecture (D) organizes data within a data lake into Bronze/Silver/Gold quality layers — it is a data lake pattern, not the full end-to-end architecture from ingestion through visualization.

ul.li: The modern data warehouse in Azure typically uses: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (raw data lake), Azure Data Factory or Synapse Pipelines (ETL/ELT orchestration), Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools (data warehouse), and Power BI (visualization and reporting).

Azure Synapse Analytics is designed to be the hub of the modern data warehouse architecture — it can serve as both the pipeline orchestrator (Synapse Pipelines) and the warehouse (dedicated SQL pools), with native integration to ADLS Gen2 and Power BI.

The modern data warehouse pattern supports both batch and interactive analytics: batch pipelines load curated data into the warehouse on schedule, while serverless SQL pools enable ad-hoc exploration of raw data lake files without waiting for the ETL to complete.

On the DP-900 exam, the modern data warehouse is the most frequently tested architecture pattern. Know the data flow: sources then data lake (raw) then pipelines (transform) then data warehouse (curated) then Power BI (visualize). Each Azure service maps to one step in this flow.
